We first recall the usual Bouncy Particle Sampler (BPS) for readers
unfamiliar with the construction [5]. It is a
piecewise-deterministic Markov process on phase space
$(x,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , where $p$ denotes velocity (equivalently,
momentum for unit mass). Its invariant distribution is
$\mu\otimes\varphi$ , where $\varphi=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ . Between events, the
particle moves along a straight line with constant $p$ :

$\dot{x}_{t}=p_{t}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\dot{p}_{t}=0\,.$

(2.1)

At state $(x,p)$ , a bounce occurs at rate

$\lambda_{\rm BPS}(x,p)\coloneqq[p^{\top}\nabla V(x)]_{+}\,.$

(2.2)

Equivalently, conditional on the current state and in the absence of a
velocity refresh, the next bounce time $\tau_{\rm b}$ satisfies

$\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\rm b}>t\mid x,p)=\exp\Bigl\{-\int_{0}^{t}[p^{\top}\nabla V(x+sp)]_{+}\,\mathrm{d}s\Bigr\}\,.$

(2.3)

At a bounce, the position is unchanged and the velocity is specularly
reflected against the gradient. For non-zero $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , set

$R_{h}\coloneqq I-2\,\frac{hh^{\top}}{\|h\|^{2}}\,,\hskip 20.00003ptR_{0}\coloneqq I\,.$

(2.4)

The bounce update is $p\leftarrow R_{\nabla V(x)}p$ . It preserves
$\|p\|$ , leaves the component tangent to a level set unchanged, and
reverses the normal component, since
$(R_{h}p)^{\top}h=-p^{\top}h$ . Thus, the particle travels freely
while moving down the potential and bounces, at a rate equal to its
instantaneous uphill directional derivative, when it moves up the
potential. Proximal BPS reuses this bounce mechanism, applied to a localized
conditional target; the construction is given in Section 3.

The standard bouncy particle sampler also uses independent velocity refreshes to ensure ergodicity, at which $p$ is redrawn from $\varphi$ . Writing

$(\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}f)(x,p)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x,p^{\prime})\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}p^{\prime})\,,$

the full generator of BPS is

$\begin{split}(\mathsf{L}_{\rm BPS}f)(x,p)&=p^{\top}\nabla_{x}f(x,p)+[p^{\top}\nabla V(x)]_{+}\{f(x,R_{\nabla V(x)}p)-f(x,p)\}+\gamma(\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}f-f)(x,p)\,.\end{split}$

(2.5)

For every refresh rate $\gamma\geq 0$ , the process with
generator (2.5) leaves
$\mu\otimes\varphi$ invariant [5], and its position
marginal is the desired target $\mu$ .

A standard way to simulate the inhomogeneous event clock
(2.3) is Poisson
thinning [18]. Suppose that, along the current deterministic segment, the
rate $\lambda(\cdot)$ is bounded above by a constant $\bar{\lambda}$ .
Generate candidate times from a homogeneous Poisson process of rate
$\bar{\lambda}$ and accept a candidate at time $t$ with probability
$\lambda(t)/\bar{\lambda}$ ; a rejected candidate causes no jump, and
the deterministic trajectory continues. The accepted times then have rate
$\lambda(\cdot)$ , so this
procedure simulates the event clock exactly. Note that only at each candidate time, one needs to query the potential gradients. If no
convenient dominating bound is available, accepting instead with
probability $\min\{1,\lambda(t)/\bar{\lambda}\}$ exactly simulates the
truncated rate $\min\{\lambda(t),\bar{\lambda}\}$ ; the only
approximation is then the replacement of the original rate by its
truncation. This is used in
Section 4.2.

Our algorithm operates on the augmented distribution underlying the
proximal sampler of Lee, Shen, and Tian [17]. For a
scale $\eta\in(0,1/\beta]$ , consider the joint law

$\pi_{\eta}(\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y)\propto\exp\Bigl\{-V(x)-\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\Bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,.$

(2.6)

The original proximal sampler algorithm performs Gibbs sampling on $\pi_{\eta}$ .
Namely, under $\pi_{\eta}$ one may generate the joint state as

$X\sim\mu\,,\hskip 20.00003ptZ\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\ \text{independently}\,,\hskip 20.00003ptY=X+\sqrt{\eta}\,Z\,.$

(2.7)

Its $X$ -marginal is $\pi_{\eta}^{X}=\mu$ . Write $\pi_{\eta}^{Y}$ for
the $Y$ -marginal, so that
$\pi_{\eta}^{Y}(\mathrm{d}y)\propto e^{-U_{\eta}(y)}\,\mathrm{d}y$ ; by
(2.7), $\pi_{\eta}^{Y}=\mu*\mathcal{N}(0,\eta I)$
is a Gaussian smoothing of the target.
We use superscripts for marginal and conditional laws; in particular,

$\pi_{\eta}^{Y\mid X=x}=\mathcal{N}(x,\eta I)\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\exp\Bigl\{-V(x)-\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\Bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}x\,.$

(2.8)

Gibbs sampling alternates exact draws from the two conditional laws in
(2.8).
The scale $\eta$ controls the strength of the quadratic coupling
potential.
Decreasing $\eta$ makes $X$ and $Y$ more tightly coupled and the
conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ more localized and better
conditioned, which reduces the cost of conditional sampling. The
resulting transitions are also more local, however, and generally require
more Gibbs sampling iterations. Thus $\eta$ balances the cost of each
iteration against the number of iterations.
The convergence and query
complexity are studied further in
[6, 9, 15].

The next proposition collects the basic geometric properties of the
augmented distribution used throughout the paper: the curvature and
concentration of the conditional law, the curvature of the
$Y$ -marginal, and a reflection symmetry of the joint law.

Proposition 2.1 (Geometry of the joint law).

The joint law (2.6) has the following properties.

(i)

For every $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the conditional law
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ has potential (that is, negative
log-density up to an additive constant)

$V_{y}(x)\coloneqq V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\,.$

(2.9)

This conditional potential satisfies

$(\alpha+\eta^{-1})I\preceq\nabla^{2}V_{y}(x)\preceq(\beta+\eta^{-1})I\,,$

(2.10)

so its condition number is at most
$(1+\beta\eta)/(1+\alpha\eta)\leq 2$ . Consequently, for every
smooth $f$ ,

$\Var_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(f)\leq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}\|\nabla f\|^{2}\,,$

(2.11)

and

$\frac{\eta}{1+\beta\eta}I\preceq\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(X)\preceq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}I\,.$

(2.12)

(ii)

The $Y$ -marginal potential satisfies

$\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha\eta}I\preceq\nabla^{2}U_{\eta}(y)\preceq\frac{\beta}{1+\beta\eta}I\,.$

(2.13)

(iii)

The state-space reflection

$\mathsf{U}:(x,y)\mapsto(x,2x-y)$

(2.14)

preserves $\pi_{\eta}$ and is an involution.

The joint law (2.6) has the following properties.

(i)

For every $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the conditional law
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ has potential (that is, negative
log-density up to an additive constant)

$V_{y}(x)\coloneqq V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\,.$

(2.9)

This conditional potential satisfies

$(\alpha+\eta^{-1})I\preceq\nabla^{2}V_{y}(x)\preceq(\beta+\eta^{-1})I\,,$

(2.10)

so its condition number is at most
$(1+\beta\eta)/(1+\alpha\eta)\leq 2$ . Consequently, for every
smooth $f$ ,

$\Var_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(f)\leq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}\|\nabla f\|^{2}\,,$

(2.11)

and

$\frac{\eta}{1+\beta\eta}I\preceq\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(X)\preceq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}I\,.$

(2.12)

(ii)

The $Y$ -marginal potential satisfies

$\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha\eta}I\preceq\nabla^{2}U_{\eta}(y)\preceq\frac{\beta}{1+\beta\eta}I\,.$

(2.13)

(iii)

The state-space reflection

$\mathsf{U}:(x,y)\mapsto(x,2x-y)$

(2.14)

preserves $\pi_{\eta}$ and is an involution.

For every $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the conditional law
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ has potential (that is, negative
log-density up to an additive constant)

$V_{y}(x)\coloneqq V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\,.$

(2.9)

This conditional potential satisfies

$(\alpha+\eta^{-1})I\preceq\nabla^{2}V_{y}(x)\preceq(\beta+\eta^{-1})I\,,$

(2.10)

so its condition number is at most
$(1+\beta\eta)/(1+\alpha\eta)\leq 2$ . Consequently, for every
smooth $f$ ,

$\Var_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(f)\leq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}\|\nabla f\|^{2}\,,$

(2.11)

and

$\frac{\eta}{1+\beta\eta}I\preceq\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}}(X)\preceq\frac{\eta}{1+\alpha\eta}I\,.$

(2.12)

The state-space reflection

$\mathsf{U}:(x,y)\mapsto(x,2x-y)$

(2.14)

preserves $\pi_{\eta}$ and is an involution.

The Hessian
bound in part (i) follows immediately from (1.1); the
Poincaré and covariance bounds then follow from the standard
log-concavity facts (D.6) and
Lemma D.3 in Appendix D, applied with
$m=\alpha+\eta^{-1}$ and $L=\beta+\eta^{-1}$ . The
marginal curvature bound in part (ii) is derived in
Appendix D, at (D.10). The
reflection statement follows directly from (2.6).

We use the standard proximal map convention of
Moreau [24]:

$\operatorname{prox}_{\eta V}(y)\coloneqq\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Bigl\{V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\Bigr\}\,.$

(2.15)

The minimizer is unique under (1.1). The objective
minimized here is exactly the conditional potential
(2.9), so $\operatorname{prox}_{\eta V}(y)$ is the
mode of $\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ ; the conditional draw is in this
sense a stochastic analogue of a proximal step, whence the
terminology arises. This exact minimizer is used below only in the analysis; the implementable algorithm never evaluates it and
does not assume access to a proximal oracle.
We use the following
conditional sampling primitive, introduced in [17].

Definition 2.2 (Restricted Gaussian oracle).

For $\eta>0$ , a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) takes input
$y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and, using fresh randomness, returns a sample with law
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ .

For $\eta>0$ , a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) takes input
$y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and, using fresh randomness, returns a sample with law
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ .

For probability measures $P\ll Q$ and $s>1$ , define the Rényi
divergence11
1

Our notation $D_{s}(P\|Q)$
corresponds to $\mathcal{R}_{s}(P\|Q)$ in [11, Definition 2.2.23], with the same definition
and normalization; we use $D_{s}$ here to avoid possible confusion with the reflection operator $R_{h}$ defined in (2.4). of order $s$ and the $\chi^{2}$ -divergence by

$D_{s}(P\|Q)\coloneqq\frac{1}{s-1}\log\int\Bigl(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}Q}\Bigr)^{s}\,\mathrm{d}Q\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\chi^{2}(P\|Q)\coloneqq e^{D_{2}(P\|Q)}-1\,.$

(2.16)

We set $D_{s}(P\|Q)=+\infty$ when $P\not\ll Q$ . We refer to a
bound $D_{2}(P\|Q)\leq\Delta$ as an order-2 Rényi
warm start bound. Our convention for total variation is
$\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\coloneqq\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ .
We use the standard inequality

$\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\leq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\chi^{2}(P\|Q)}\,.$

(2.17)

For any coupling $(X,Y)$ of $P$ and $Q$ ,
$\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\leq\mathbb{P}\{X\neq Y\}$ , and a maximal coupling of $X$ and $Y$ attains
equality.

If $X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ and, conditionally on $X_{0}$ ,
$Y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(X_{0},\eta I)$ , then, whenever $\mu_{0}\ll\mu$ ,

$\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}(X_{0},Y_{0})}{\mathrm{d}\pi_{\eta}}(x,y)=\frac{\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}(x)\,.$

Consequently,

$D_{2}\bigl(\mathcal{L}(X_{0},Y_{0})\|\pi_{\eta}\bigr)=D_{2}(\mu_{0}\|\mu)\,.$

(2.18)

The identity also holds in the extended sense when
$\mu_{0}\not\ll\mu$ , in which case both sides are infinite.

Notation.

For a random variable $W$ , $\mathcal{L}(W)$ denotes its law, and
for a probability measure $P$ on a product space, $P^{X}$ denotes
its $X$ -marginal. Markov kernels are denoted by calligraphic
symbols. If $\mathcal{K}$ is a Markov kernel,
$P\mathcal{K}$ denotes the law obtained by applying $\mathcal{K}$ to
$P$ , and $\mathcal{K}^{m}$ denotes its $m$ -fold iterate. Linear operators and state-space transformations are denoted by
sans-serif symbols, scalar functionals by script letters, and
finite-dimensional matrices by ordinary uppercase symbols. We write
$[u]_{+}\coloneqq\max\{u,0\}$ . The notation $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm for
vectors, the induced operator norm for matrices and bounded linear
operators, and the ambient $L^{2}$ -norm for functions; inner products
are interpreted analogously from context. Unsubscripted letters
$c,C>0$ denote universal constants whose values may change from line
to line, while constants denoted by $K$ , with or without a
descriptive subscript, are fixed within the result in which they are
introduced. The notation $\widetilde{O}(B)$ means $B$ times a
fixed universal power of logarithms in the displayed problem
parameters; no polynomial dependence is hidden.

Fix $Y=y$ . Recall from (2.8) that the position
$X$ to be sampled has conditional law

$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x)\propto e^{-V_{y}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x\,,\hskip 20.00003ptV_{y}(x)\coloneqq V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}}{2\eta}\,.$

We construct the half-turn process so that its induced transition
preserves this law. The
construction starts from vanilla BPS for the conditional target, absorbs
the quadratic coupling potential into the deterministic motion, and then
introduces
an independent conditional reference point to localize the remaining
bounce rate. We begin by introducing a Gaussian momentum
$p\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ . The phase space law to be preserved is

$\nu_{\eta,y}(\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p)\coloneqq\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)(\mathrm{d}p)\propto\exp\Bigl\{-V_{y}(x)-\frac{\|p\|^{2}}{2}\Bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\,.$

(3.1)

Recall from (2.4) that $R_{h}$ denotes specular
reflection across the hyperplane orthogonal to $h$ .

A natural first attempt is to apply vanilla BPS directly to this
conditional distribution. Its infinitesimal generator acts on a smooth
test function $f$ as

$\begin{split}(\mathsf{L}_{y}^{\rm vanilla}f)(x,p)&=\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}\nabla_{x}f(x,p)\\
&\quad+\sqrt{\eta}\,[p^{\top}\nabla V_{y}(x)]_{+}\bigl\{f(x,R_{\nabla V_{y}(x)}p)-f(x,p)\bigr\}\,.\end{split}$

(3.2)

The common factor $\sqrt{\eta}$ only fixes the unit of time; it does not
change the invariant law. We choose this unit so that the harmonic motion
introduced below has period $2\pi$ .
The first term gives straight-line motion, while the second reflects the
momentum against the full conditional gradient. This process is exact,
but it can be expensive: even when $V=0$ , the quadratic coupling potential
$\|{\cdot}-y\|^{2}/(2\eta)$ produces a stationary mean bounce rate of order
$\sqrt{d}$ .

To reduce the number of bounce events, we put the quadratic part of the
conditional gradient into the deterministic dynamics. This gives the
generator

$\begin{split}(\mathsf{L}_{y}^{\rm harm}f)(x,p)&=\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}\nabla_{x}f(x,p)-\frac{(x-y)^{\top}}{\sqrt{\eta}}\nabla_{p}f(x,p)\\
&\quad+\sqrt{\eta}\,[p^{\top}\nabla V(x)]_{+}\bigl\{f(x,R_{\nabla V(x)}p)-f(x,p)\bigr\}\,.\end{split}$

(3.3)

The first line is the Hamiltonian flow associated with the quadratic
coupling potential: between bounces, it rotates $(x-y)/\sqrt{\eta}$ and
$p$ . This use of a quadratic reference flow, with the remaining force
handled by bounce events, is analogous to the Boomerang
sampler [4].
The direct harmonic generator (3.3)
still bounces against the full gradient $\nabla V$ , so its bounce rate
can remain large.

To further reduce the bounce rate and the resulting computational
cost, we introduce a conditional reference point and use the smoothness of
$V$ to control the local gradient difference. Specifically, draw
$\widetilde{X}\sim\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ independently and write the exact
decomposition

$\nabla V(x)=\nabla V(\widetilde{X})+\{\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(\widetilde{X})\}\,.$

Conditionally on $\widetilde{X}=\widetilde{x}$ , we incorporate the fixed
reference term into the deterministic dynamics and retain only the gradient
difference in the BPS jump term. Define the equilibrium position of this
deterministic harmonic flow and the residual gradient by

$c_{y,\widetilde{x}}\coloneqq y-\eta\nabla V(\widetilde{x})\,,\hskip 20.00003pth_{\widetilde{x}}(x)\coloneqq\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(\widetilde{x})\,.$

(3.4)

The resulting generator is

$\begin{split}\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}f(x,p)&\coloneqq\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}\nabla_{x}f(x,p)-\frac{(x-c_{y,\widetilde{x}})^{\top}}{\sqrt{\eta}}\nabla_{p}f(x,p)\\
&\quad+\sqrt{\eta}\,[p^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)]_{+}\bigl\{f(x,R_{h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)}p)-f(x,p)\bigr\}\,.\end{split}$

(3.5)

The harmonic and residual terms sum to the full conditional force
$\sqrt{\eta}\,\nabla V_{y}(x)$ . Thus $\widetilde{x}$ changes only how this
force is divided between deterministic motion and bounces. By the
$\beta$ -smoothness of $V$ ,

$\|h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)\|=\|\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(\widetilde{x})\|\leq\beta\,\|x-\widetilde{x}\|\,.$

Drawing the reference point from the same localized conditional law keeps
the residual gradient small and reduces the expected number of bounces per
run of the half-turn process to order $\beta\eta\sqrt{d}$ ; see
Proposition 3.3.

Having specified the dynamics, it remains to choose the integration
horizon. For fixed $(y,\widetilde{x})$ , the deterministic part of
(3.5) is harmonic motion about its equilibrium
position $c_{y,\widetilde{x}}$ . In the absence of bounces, its position at
time $t$ satisfies

$x_{t}-c_{y,\widetilde{x}}=(x_{0}-c_{y,\widetilde{x}})\cos t+\sqrt{\eta}\,p_{0}\sin t\,.$

(3.6)

As discussed earlier, we choose the integration horizon $t=\pi$ , corresponding to one
half-period. This is the first non-zero harmonic time at which the
position $x_{\pi}$ no longer depends on the initial momentum $p_{0}$ .
Without bounces, the resulting map is

$(x_{\pi},p_{\pi})=(2c_{y,\widetilde{x}}-x_{0},-p_{0})\,.$

(3.7)

Thus, the position is reflected through the equilibrium position

The construction is now complete. The following algorithm gives its
pathwise prescription: it draws the reference point and momentum, evolves
the process with generator (3.5) for time $\pi$ , and
returns only the final position.

Algorithm 1 Simulation of the ideal conditional half-turn process

1:

Input: state $(x,y)$

2:

Draw $\widetilde{X}\sim\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ and
$p_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ independently.

3:

Query $\nabla V(\widetilde{X})$ .

4:

Set $x_{0}\leftarrow x$ .

5:

Evolve $(x_{t},p_{t})$ according to

$\dot{x}=\sqrt{\eta}\,p\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\dot{p}=-\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{\eta}}-\sqrt{\eta}\,\nabla V(\widetilde{X})\,,$

(3.8)

until $t=\pi$ .

6:

During the evolution, generate bounce events at rate

$\lambda_{\widetilde{X}}(x,p)=\sqrt{\eta}\,\bigl[p^{\top}[\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(\widetilde{X})]\bigr]_{+}\,.$

(3.9)

7:

At each bounce, set
$p_{t}\leftarrow R_{\nabla V(x_{t})-\nabla V(\widetilde{X})}p_{t}$ .

8:

return $x_{\pi}$

Proposition 3.1 (Well-posedness and stationarity of the conditional phase space process).

For every fixed $y,\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and initial phase space point
$(x_{0},p_{0})$ , the event-driven dynamics in Algorithm 1, with
the reference point fixed at $\widetilde{x}$ , defines a unique
non-explosive, time-homogeneous Markov process. The phase space measure
$\nu_{\eta,y}$ is stationary for this process. In particular, the
returned position $x_{\pi}$ is well-defined almost surely.

The well-posedness and stationarity assertions are proved in
Section A.1.

The induced Markov kernel on positions also satisfies the following
reversibility property.

Proposition 3.2 (Reversibility of the conditional half-turn kernel).

For every $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , let $\mathcal{H}_{y}$ be the Markov kernel on
$\mathbb{R}^{d}$ induced by Algorithm 1; thus
$\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,\cdot)$ is the law of the returned position $x_{\pi}$
for input $(x,y)$ . Then $\mathcal{H}_{y}$ is reversible with respect to
$\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ .
The proof is deferred to Appendix A.2.

The following proposition quantifies the stationary bounce count of the

Proposition 3.3 (Stationary bounce count).

in the resulting ideal half-turn process of Algorithm 1, then

$\mathbb{E}N_{\rm b}^{\rm id}\leq K_{\rm id}\beta\eta\sqrt{d}\,.$

To prove non-explosion, define the shifted harmonic energy

$H_{y,\widetilde{x}}(x,p)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\,\bigl\{\eta^{-1}\,\|x-c_{y,\widetilde{x}}\|^{2}+\|p\|^{2}\bigr\}\,.$

The flow and each bounce preserve this energy. Hence, with
$\mathcal{E}\coloneqq H_{y,\widetilde{x}}(x_{0},p_{0})$ , every state produced by
the recursion satisfies

$\|p\|\leq\sqrt{2\mathcal{E}}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\|x-c_{y,\widetilde{x}}\|\leq\sqrt{2\eta\mathcal{E}}\,.$

Because $\nabla V$ is $\beta$ -Lipschitz,
$\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p)\leq\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})$ throughout the path, where

$\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})\coloneqq\sqrt{\eta}\,\beta\sqrt{2\mathcal{E}}\,\bigl\{\sqrt{2\eta\mathcal{E}}+\|c_{y,\widetilde{x}}-\widetilde{x}\|\bigr\}\,.$

Hence,

$\int_{0}^{u}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\Phi_{s}^{y,\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{T_{n}}))\,\mathrm{d}s\leq\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})\,u\,.$

If $\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})=0$ , the event rate
vanishes and there are no jumps. Otherwise,
(A.1) implies, for every finite waiting time,

$S_{n+1}\geq\frac{E_{n+1}}{\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})}\,.$

If the recursion does not terminate, it follows that

$T_{n}\geq\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}E_{j}}{\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})}\longrightarrow\infty$

almost surely by the strong law of large numbers. Thus, the jump times
cannot accumulate, and the recursive construction defines a unique
process for all $t\geq 0$ . Finally, the
memoryless property of the exponential clocks gives the time-homogeneous
Markov property. This is precisely the integrated hazard construction
of Davis [12, Section 2].

With the process now constructed, we prove the stationarity assertion in
Proposition 3.1 and record the stronger operator facts used
to analyze the averaged kernel. Recall $\nu_{\eta,y}$ from
(3.1), and define momentum
reversal by

$\mathsf{R}(x,p)\coloneqq(x,-p)\,,\hskip 20.00003pt(\mathsf{R}F)(x,p)\coloneqq F(\mathsf{R}(x,p))\,.$

As usual, we use the same symbol for $\nu_{\eta,y}$ and its Lebesgue
density:

$\nu_{\eta,y}(x,p)\propto\exp\Bigl\{-V_{y}(x)-\frac{\|p\|^{2}}{2}\Bigr\}\,.$

Idea of the proof.

The identity (A.3) is a
momentum-reversed form of detailed balance. To see the mechanism
formally, write
$\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}=\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{J}$ , where

$\displaystyle\mathcal{A}f(x,p)$
$\displaystyle\coloneqq\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}\nabla_{x}f(x,p)-\frac{(x-c_{y,\widetilde{x}})^{\top}}{\sqrt{\eta}}\nabla_{p}f(x,p),$

$\displaystyle\mathcal{J}f(x,p)$
$\displaystyle\coloneqq\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p)\bigl\{f(\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p))-f(x,p)\bigr\}.$

Momentum reversal reverses the harmonic flow, so
$\mathsf{R}\mathcal{A}\mathsf{R}=-\mathcal{A}$ . Moreover,

$\mathcal{A}\log\nu_{\eta,y}(x,p)=-\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)=-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p)+\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,-p).$

Formal integration by parts gives

$\mathcal{A}^{*}=-\mathcal{A}+\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R}.$

The bounce map $\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}$ is a
$\nu_{\eta,y}$ -preserving involution, commutes with $\mathsf{R}$ , and
satisfies $\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}=\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R}$ . A formal change of variables
therefore gives

$\mathcal{J}^{*}G=(\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R})(G\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}})-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}G.$

Combining the two identities yields

$\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}^{*}G=-\mathcal{A}G+(\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R})(G\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}-G)=(\mathsf{R}\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R})G.$

Formally exponentiating this identity gives
$(\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}})^{*}=\mathsf{R}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}$ ; Gaussian momentum averaging
then removes $\mathsf{R}$ and produces an ordinary self-adjoint position
kernel.

This generator calculation is only heuristic as stated, as the standard arguments are not
immediately applicable because
$\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}$ may be discontinuous where
$h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)=0$ . The pathwise argument below proves the same
identity without requiring differentiability or continuity of the
bounce map.

Proof.

Along
$\zeta_{s}=(x_{s},p_{s})=\Phi_{s}^{y,\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{0})$ ,

$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\log\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{s})=-\sqrt{\eta}\,p_{s}^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x_{s})=-\bigl\{\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s})-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{s})\bigr\}\,.$

(A.4)

Moreover, by definition of $\mathsf{R}$ and $\Phi_{t}$ ,

$\mathsf{R}\Phi_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}=\Phi_{-t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathsf{R}\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}=\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}\,.$

If $\zeta^{+}=\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}\zeta^{-}$ is a non-trivial jump, then
$h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)\neq 0$ ,
$(p^{-})^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)>0$ , and

$\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta^{-})=\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta^{+})\,.$

(A.5)

The flow and $\mathsf{R}$ preserve Lebesgue measure, as does the possibly
discontinuous bounce map: by Fubini’s theorem and orthogonality, for
every integrable $F$ ,

$\int F(\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p))\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p=\int F(x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\,.$

(A.6)

To pass from these identities to complete trajectories, let

$\Delta_{n}(t)\coloneqq\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}):0

Given $\zeta_{0}$ and $\mathbf{t}\in\Delta_{n}(t)$ , let
$\zeta_{s}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}}$ be the path obtained by following
$\Phi^{y,\widetilde{x}}$ and applying $\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}$ at the
prescribed times. Iterating the exponential clock construction gives,
for every bounded measurable functional $\Psi$ of the path up to time
$t$ ,

$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\zeta_{0}}\Psi(\zeta_{[0,t]})$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int_{\Delta_{n}(t)}\Psi(\zeta_{[0,t]}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\exp\Bigl\{-\!\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\,\mathrm{d}s\Bigr\}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{t_{j}-}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}\,.$

(A.7)

The series is absolutely convergent because
$\lvert\Delta_{n}(t)\rvert=t^{n}/n!$ and the rate
is bounded by $\bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x})$ .
Integrate (A.7) against
$\nu_{\eta,y}(\mathrm{d}\zeta_{0})$ and apply

$(\zeta_{s})_{0\leq s\leq t}\longmapsto(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{t-s})_{0\leq s\leq t}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n})\longmapsto(t-t_{n},\ldots,t-t_{1})\,.$

(A.8)

For completeness, we justify this change of variables despite the
possible discontinuity of the bounce map. For fixed
$\mathbf{t}\in\Delta_{n}(t)$ , the endpoint map
$\zeta_{0}\mapsto\zeta_{t}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}}$ is a finite composition
of the Borel involution $\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}$ and the affine
harmonic flows $\Phi_{u}^{y,\widetilde{x}}$ . By
(A.6) and the explicit flow formula, each factor is
a measure-preserving Borel bijection. Hence the endpoint map, and
therefore
$\zeta_{0}\mapsto\mathsf{R}\zeta_{t}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}}$ , is a Borel
measure-preserving bijection. The identities preceding
(A.7) show that its inverse is obtained by
using the reversed ordered times in (A.8). The
map on $\Delta_{n}(t)$ is linear with absolute determinant one.
Thus the full change of variables is measure preserving; no Jacobian is needed.

Integrating (A.4) over the deterministic arcs
and using that a reflection preserves $\nu_{\eta,y}$ gives

$\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{0})\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s}=\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{t})\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s}\,.$

This identity matches the initial density and survival factor of a
forward path with those of its reversal, while
(A.5) matches every jump-rate factor. Hence,
each $n$ -jump term in (A.7) is unchanged by
(A.8). Tonelli’s theorem justifies the termwise
change of variables for non-negative bounded functions; decomposing
signed functions into positive and negative parts then gives, for
bounded measurable $F,G$ ,

$\int F\,\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}G\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\eta,y}=\int(\mathsf{R}G)\,\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}F)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\eta,y}\,.$

Taking $F=1$ proves invariance, and the identity extends by density to
(A.3) on $L^{2}(\nu_{\eta,y})$ .

Invariance and Jensen’s inequality give
$\|\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}F\|_{2}\leq\|F\|_{2}$ . It remains to prove
strong continuity. For $F\in C_{\rm c}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})$ , the deterministic flow

$t$ is

$1-\exp\Bigl\{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\Phi_{s}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\zeta)\,\mathrm{d}s\Bigr\}\longrightarrow 0\,.$

Dominated convergence therefore gives
$\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}F\to F$ in $L^{2}$ . Density of
$C_{\rm c}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})$ and contractivity extend this to all $F\in L^{2}$ .

Finally, Gaussian momentum averaging satisfies
$\mathsf{R}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}$ and
$\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{R}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}$ . Combining these identities with
(A.3) gives

$(\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*})^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}(\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}})^{*}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{R}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}\,.$

This proves self-adjointness; the Markov and contraction properties are
inherited from $\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}$ .
